idiom_name: hand-written decode/pack functions over a canonical struct (byteorder + a text/JSON helper)
implementation_notes: ISO C has no reflection and no serialisation layer, so the translator is a pair of hand-written functions: one parses the foreign wire form (fixed-width fields, delimited text, or JSON via a library such as Jansson) into a canonical struct, the other re-encodes that struct into the receiver's format. Numeric fields need explicit byte-order conversion with htons/ntohs and htonl/ntohl whenever the wire order differs from the host's, and strings need explicit length, encoding and terminator handling. The classic Translator class therefore collapses into one struct (the canonical model) plus two module-level functions; a dedicated translator object is only worth building in C when the mapping needs runtime state such as loaded code lists.
pitfalls: Byte order and alignment: casting a char buffer to uint32_t* violates alignment and silently mismatches the wire order - copy through memcpy or read bytes and convert with ntohl.
Fixed-width extraction without bounds checks reads past the buffer; unbounded strcpy/strcpy-family copies in the mapping are the classic overrun in a translator.
Errors must be returned, not ignored: a function that writes a partly filled struct on failure propagates garbage into the canonical model that looks like valid data.
